problem: Navigation methods define success as being near the target and ignore whether the stopping pose allows manipulation (reach, clutter, obstacles). Existing datasets give little supervision for this 'last-mile' positioning, and training-free LLM approaches cannot adapt to different arms or base heights.
motivation: In mobile manipulation, navigation is only a step before manipulation. A robot that stops out of reach or blocked by furniture cannot execute the task. Learning where on the floor manipulation is feasible, conditioned on the robot's arm and base, needs large-scale, automatically labelled data.
key_idea: Build a 127k-episode simulated kitchen benchmark whose ground truth is dense floor-level affordance maps from real grasp attempts by different mobile manipulators, and train a point-cloud model (NavAff) to predict those maps from first-person RGB-D.
insight: Both scene context and 2D semantic cues matter. Removing the global point cloud drops PCC from 0.680 to 0.534 and top1 MSR from 0.72 to 0.58. Removing VAM (target/obstacle channels) drops PCC to 0.562 and MSR to 0.63. Robot information has only a small effect (PCC 0.670, MSR 0.70), which the authors attribute to using only two parameters and to most platforms sharing a base height. Across methods, better affordance metrics go with higher manipulation success.
method: Scene generation: In BestMan (PyBullet) with PartNet-Mobility assets, kitchen furniture is arranged procedurally along a wall. 1-3 rigid targets, articulated targets and 1-3 obstacles per target are added, giving 569 scenes and 127,343 episodes.

Affordance labeling: Base positions are sampled every 10 cm in a semicircle of radius equal to arm reach around the target. At each, the end-effector is aligned to the surface normal, a grasp or suction is attempted, and a binary success is recorded. Six arms are used: Flexiv, Panda, UR5e, xArm6, Realman, Elephant.

Dense map creation: Binary labels are transformed to the camera/base frame, matched to floor point-cloud points by nearest neighbor within a threshold, then Gaussian-weighted kNN interpolation gives dense values in [0,1].
Visual data: 10 first-person camera poses per configuration provide RGB, depth, global point cloud and floor point cloud (z>0.02 m).
Visual Alignment Module (VAM): Target and obstacle masks from BestMan are back-projected onto the global point cloud as extra channels (+1 for target, -1 for obstacles) and processed by PointNet++.

Navigation Affordance Grounding (NAG): PointNet++ features of the global and floor clouds are tokenized. Floor tokens act as queries in multi-head cross-attention over the global tokens concatenated with robot tokens (base height and arm radius via MLP), and a decoder predicts per-point affordance.
Weighted MSE loss: Zero-valued labels are down-weighted by lambda with probability 0.5 to handle class imbalance. The best value is around 0.7 by PCC.

setting.backbone: NavAff: PointNet++ encoders + MLP tokenizers + multi-head cross-attention + decoder (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: MoMa-Kitchen train split: 456 scenes, 11,408 configurations, 102,687 episodes (simulation only)
setting.observation: first-person RGB-D from an arm-mounted camera, back-projected to global and floor point clouds, plus target/obstacle masks and robot parameters (base height, arm reach)
setting.action_space: none; predicts a dense floor affordance map from which a stopping position is chosen (top-1/top-5)
setting.privileged: GT target/obstacle masks from the simulator (BestMan) in simulation; real-world uses Grounded-SAM masks and Depth Anything v2 depth

numbers.extra: test split of 113 unseen scenes, 24,656 episodes; top1 MSR is a separate simulated-execution metric
numbers.evidence: Table 2 Main results; Table 3 Manipulation Success Rate (Top1 0.72, Top5 0.66)

numbers_note: Only the paper's own benchmark is reported. No standard navigation benchmarks. Real-world results are qualitative only.
results: NavAff beats the adapted baselines PointNet++ (RMSE 0.164, PCC 0.565), VoteNet and H3DNet on all affordance metrics. It reaches top1 MSR 0.72 versus 0.60 for PointNet++ and 0.080 for random. A qualitative real-world demo transfers from simulation.
limitations: Kitchen scenes only, and only reaching/grasping (or suction) tasks.
Robot information is limited to two parameters (base height, arm radius), which makes the model's use of it weak; baselines are adapted point-cloud models rather than dedicated methods.
Sim-to-real is shown only qualitatively, using Grounded-SAM and Depth Anything to produce inputs.
